osce_examination.title: Upper-Limb Neurovascular Examination After Humeral Fracture
osce_examination.related_topic: Arm trauma, radial nerve examination, and distal neurovascular assessment
osce_examination.candidate_instructions: Assess the upper-limb neurovascular status of a patient with a suspected humeral fracture. Explain the examination, compare both limbs, and document the findings.
osce_examination.patient_scenario: A 67-year-old woman presents with severe upper-arm pain and swelling after falling on an outstretched hand. The case describes mid-arm tenderness and radial nerve palsy.

examination_steps.heading: Preparation and initial trauma assessment
actions: Introduce yourself, confirm the patient's identity, explain the examination and obtain consent.
Perform hand hygiene and ensure appropriate exposure and privacy.
In a trauma patient, begin with the ABCDE approach before focusing on the fracture.
Avoid passive movement in this acute injury scenario.

examination_steps.heading: Inspection
actions: Inspect the affected upper limb for swelling, bruising/ecchymosis, deformity and skin colour changes.
Observe the position in which the patient holds the arm.
Compare with the unaffected limb.

examination_steps.heading: Vascular assessment
actions: Assess hand colour and temperature.
Assess capillary refill.
Palpate the brachial and radial pulses and compare with the unaffected side.
Pay particular attention to the neurovascular bundle, including the deep brachial artery in a humeral shaft injury.

examination_steps.heading: Radial nerve assessment
actions: Test elbow flexion strength through brachioradialis function.
Test triceps strength and elbow extension.
Ask the patient to extend the wrist.
Ask the patient to extend the fingers and MCP joints.
Assess sensation over the dorsum of the hand, including the anatomical snuffbox area.
Check the triceps tendon jerk.

examination_steps.heading: Median nerve assessment
actions: Ask the patient to make an OK sign.
Assess relevant median nerve motor function.
Test sensation in the median nerve sensory distribution.

examination_steps.heading: Ulnar nerve assessment
actions: Ask the patient to abduct and adduct the fingers.
Test sensation over the ulnar side of the hand.

examination_steps.heading: Comparison, documentation and reassessment
actions: Compare motor, sensory and vascular findings with the unaffected limb.
Document the findings clearly, including any deficit and the time of assessment.
Repeat the neurovascular assessment after immobilization.

expected_findings: The case reports swelling and extensive ecchymosis of the upper arm with mid-arm tenderness.
Brachial and radial pulses are reported normal in the case.
Radial nerve palsy is described by inability to extend the wrist and MCP joints.
Sensory loss is reported over the anatomical snuffbox.
Median and ulnar nerve examinations are reported normal in the case.

clinical_interpretation.likely_pattern: Humeral shaft fracture associated with radial nerve palsy.
supporting_features: Mid-arm tenderness and swelling after a fall.
Sensory loss over the anatomical snuffbox.
anatomical_correlation: Midshaft humeral fracture → radial nerve injury → wrist drop.
Surgical neck fracture → axillary nerve injury.
Supracondylar fracture → possible brachial artery and median/AIN injury.

common_mistakes: Starting with the fracture rather than the ABCDE trauma approach.
Performing passive movement in the acute injury scenario.
Failing to assess both vascular and neurological status.
Omitting the median or ulnar nerve examination.
Failing to compare with the unaffected limb.
Failing to document findings or repeat the neurovascular assessment after immobilization.
critical_steps: ABCDE assessment before focused fracture management.
Assessment of brachial/radial pulses and distal perfusion.
Focused radial nerve motor, sensory and reflex examination.
Documentation and repeat neurovascular assessment after immobilization.

focused_history.candidate_instructions: Take a focused history from a patient presenting with acute upper-arm pain following a fall.

standardized_patient_profile.presenting_complaint: Upper-arm pain for 3 hours after falling on an outstretched hand.

questions: What happened immediately before the pain started?
question_sequence.purpose: Establish the site, duration and mechanism of injury.

question_sequence.purpose: Identify associated injury features and possible neurovascular symptoms.

questions: Do you have any medical conditions?
What regular medications do you take?
Do you have any drug allergies?
question_sequence.purpose: Establish comorbidities, medication use and allergies relevant to acute trauma care.

focused_history.history_summary_template: Nidhal Hassan is a 67-year-old woman presenting with 3 hours of sharp, severe (9/10), progressive upper-arm pain after falling on an outstretched hand while walking in the garden. The pain is aggravated by movement and is associated with upper-arm swelling and bluish discoloration. She reports no loss of consciousness. Her medical history includes hypertension for 10 years and ischemic heart disease for 3 years. She takes oral antihypertensive, antiplatelet and lipid-lowering medication, has no reported drug allergy, does not smoke or drink alcohol, and has a sister with multiple myeloma.
source_limitations: The standardized-patient sheet gives left arm pain in the presenting complaint but describes right-sided swelling and examination findings; the station therefore refers to the affected upper arm without assigning a side.
The source asks the student to prescribe an analgesic but does not specify a preferred drug or dose.
Responses to questions about hand numbness/tingling are not provided in the standardized-patient sheet and should be elicited rather than assumed.

osce_framework.station: Upper-limb neurovascular examination after humeral fracture
osce_framework.source_status: Integrated from the supplied Skill Lab examination sequence and user-provided examination points.
checklist: Inspect the affected arm and compare with the unaffected limb.
Assess distal perfusion and brachial/radial pulses.
Assess radial nerve motor, sensory and reflex function.
Assess median nerve motor and sensory function, including the OK sign.
Assess ulnar nerve motor and sensory function.
Document findings and repeat neurovascular assessment after immobilization.
limitations: The supplied Skill Lab states that passive movement is contraindicated in this acute trauma scenario.
The source does not provide a specific analgesic prescription or dose.
